activities.anchor: One tool from the earlier tiers gets promoted
activities.caption: pair each object with its question
activities.name: ntToolMatch

config.prompt: Pair each object with the statement that defines it:

pairs.right: a = q·b + r, with unique q and 0 ≤ r < b
gcd(a, b) = 1 — the friendly case where inverses exist

config.why: Everything on this page — gcds, clocks, cryptography — is the remainder r taken seriously as a mathematical object in its own right.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — why digit sums detect 9s
activities.name: ntDigitCloze

config.text: A number is divisible by 9 exactly when its digit sum is, because 10 ≡ %%0%% (mod 9), so 10ᵏ ≡ %%1%% for every power: 4,713 leaves the same remainder as 4 + 7 + 1 + 3 = 15 ≡ %%2%%.
config.hint: Ten is one more than nine; powers inherit it; and 15 mod 9 is…

activities.anchor: gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b
activities.caption: find the broken identity
activities.name: ntBezoutSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims is wrong — click it:
lines: gcd(a, b) can always be written as ax + by for integer x and y.
Run the Euclid steps backwards to find x and y.
gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a + b.
config.why: The identity is behind every 'find the LCM via the GCD' shortcut.

config.prompt: Roughly how many primes are there below 100?
config.why: 25 below 100, 168 below 1,000, 9,592 below 100,000 — primes thin out lawfully: the count below n is asymptotically n/ln n.
config.context: the prime number theorem was proved in 1896 by Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin

activities.caption: drop the marker — the prime density
activities.name: ntDensityPlace

config.prompt: Around 10¹⁸, about one number in how many is prime?
config.why: About 1 in 41.5 — primes get rarer but never die out, and the average gap near n is ln n.

activities.anchor: To find all primes below a limit
activities.caption: rebuild the sieve
activities.name: ntSieveOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the sieve of Eratosthenes — what comes first:
items: Write the numbers up to N
Any survivor below √N crossing is prime
config.why: To test one large number instead, probabilistic tests like Miller–Rabin do it in milliseconds without factoring anything — the asymmetry cryptography exploits.

activities.anchor: congruences can be divided through like equations
activities.caption: the illegal cancellation
activities.name: ntCancelBranch

config.root: 2·3 ≡ 4·3 (mod 6). A student cancels the 3 and concludes 2 ≡ 4 (mod 6). What went wrong?

choices.label: Nothing — cancelling is always legal
choices.feedback: Cancellation is legal only when the cancelled factor is coprime to the modulus: 3 shares a factor with 6, and the 'division' discards information about multiples of 6.

choices.label: 3 is not coprime to 6 — 'dividing' mod m means multiplying by an inverse
choices.feedback: Right — and inverses exist only for coprime factors; mod 5, where 3 is coprime to the modulus, the same cancellation works.

choices.label: The original congruence was false
choices.feedback: It is true — both sides are 0 mod 6; the illegal step is the cancellation.

wrong.text: Both sides being 0 hides the difference between 2 and 4.

right.text: Mod 7, the inverse of 3 is 5 (3 × 5 = 15 ≡ 1), so 'divide by 3' means 'multiply by 5'.

false.text: The congruence holds; the inference from it does not.

config.why: Dividing mod m really means multiplying by an inverse — and inverses exist only for coprime factors.

activities.caption: pair each modular fact with its instance
activities.name: ntFermatMatch

config.prompt: Pair each modular fact with its instance:

pairs.right: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p, a not divisible by p

config.why: Every nonzero residue's power comes home after p − 1 steps — the engine inside RSA.

activities.caption: true or false — the margin note's fate
activities.name: ntWilesJudge

config.statement: Fermat's Last Theorem was proven by Andrew Wiles in 1995 using seven chapters of elliptic-curve theory Fermat could not have dreamed of.
config.why: Conjectured in 1637 in a margin too small for the proof, proven in 1995 — a whole ocean of modern number theory grew from that margin note.

config.prompt: Rebuild the toy RSA computation — what comes first:
items: Pick primes p = 3, q = 11: n = 33, φ(n) = 20
Publish e = 3, keep d = 7 with e·d ≡ 1 (mod 20)
config.why: Fermat-and-Euler arithmetic guarantees the answer is m again — every HTTPS padlock is this postscript to Hardy's 'useless' boast.
